subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Race: Time and Speed
hook: Amir enters a village race, and discovers that time, distance, and speed are connected by math.

characters.name: Coach Raj
characters.role: village sports trainer, uses math to teach running

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Amir's cousin, keeps track of times

slides.title: Racing Seconds
slides.storyContext: The village announces a 400-meter race. Amir trains with Coach Raj, who explains: 'To win, you need to run 400 meters in the shortest time. But time and speed are connected — understanding this math will help you run faster.'

slides.title: Training Day
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj times Amir running 100 meters: 20 seconds. 'Good!' says Coach. 'Now I'll teach you about speed. Speed is distance divided by time. You ran 100 meters in 20 seconds, so your speed is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 meters per second.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells you how fast something moves. It's distance traveled divided by time taken. If you run 100 meters in 20 seconds, your speed is 5 meters per second.

slides.title: Understanding Time: Seconds, Minutes, Hours
slides.storyContext: Meera keeps a stopwatch. 'One minute is 60 seconds,' she explains. 'One hour is 60 minutes, so 3,600 seconds.' Amir practices: 20 seconds, 45 seconds, 1 minute 15 seconds (= 75 seconds).

points.label: Time Conversions
points.text: 60 seconds = 1 minute. 60 minutes = 1 hour. 1 hour = 3,600 seconds. To convert: multiply to go to smaller units (minutes to seconds), divide to go to larger units (seconds to minutes).

example.problem: Convert 2 minutes 30 seconds to just seconds. Convert 180 seconds to minutes.
example.solution: 2 min 30 sec = (2 × 60) + 30 = 120 + 30 = 150 seconds. 180 seconds ÷ 60 = 3 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply by 60 to convert minutes to seconds. Divide by 60 to convert seconds to minutes.

slides.title: Measuring Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj marks the track: '100 meters is about the length of the main street. 400 meters is one lap around our field. 1 kilometer is 1,000 meters — that's the distance from the village to the neighboring town.'

points.label: Distance Units
points.text: 1 kilometer (km) = 1,000 meters (m). 1 meter (m) = 100 centimeters (cm). In a race, we measure distances in meters and kilometers.

example.problem: A race is 2 kilometers long. How many meters?

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 km = 1,000 m. Use this conversion to switch between kilometers and meters.

slides.title: Speed = Distance ÷ Time
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj teaches the formula. 'Speed equals distance divided by time. If Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, his speed is 400 ÷ 80 = 5 meters per second.' Amir practices: 100 m in 20 sec → 5 m/s. 200 m in 50 sec → 4 m/s.

points.label: Speed Formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time. If speed is S, distance is D, and time is T, then S = D ÷ T. Units: meters per second (m/s), kilometers per hour (km/h), etc.

example.problem: A runner covers 200 meters in 40 seconds. What is the speed?
example.solution: Speed = 200 m ÷ 40 s = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed = how far ÷ how long. A runner who covers 100 m in 20 s has a speed of 5 m per second.

slides.title: Rearranging the Formula: Finding Time or Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach challenges Amir differently: 'If you want to run 400 meters at 5 m/s, how long will it take?' Amir rearranges: Time = Distance ÷ Speed = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 seconds. Later: 'If you have 60 seconds and want to run at 6 m/s, how far will you go?' Distance = Speed × Time = 6 × 60 = 360 meters.

points.label: Rearranging Speed Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time, or D = S × T. Time = Distance ÷ Speed, or T = D ÷ S.

example.problem: Amir runs at 5 m/s. How far does he run in 25 seconds? How long to run 500 meters?
example.solution: Distance: 5 × 25 = 125 meters. Time: 500 ÷ 5 = 100 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed × Time = Distance. Distance ÷ Speed = Time. Distance ÷ Time = Speed. Know any two, find the third.

slides.title: Comparing Speeds
slides.storyContext: Two runners compete: Amir (400 m in 80 s) and his friend Ravi (400 m in 100 s). Meera calculates: Amir's speed = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s. Ravi's speed = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s. 'Amir is faster!'

points.label: Comparing Speeds
points.text: Calculate speed for each runner or vehicle. The higher speed means faster movement. Use the same units to compare fairly.

example.problem: Runner A: 200 m in 40 s. Runner B: 300 m in 60 s. Who is faster?
example.solution: Runner A speed: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 m/s. Runner B speed: 300 ÷ 60 = 5 m/s. Same speed! It's a tie.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each runner's speed, then compare. Bigger speed = faster runner.

slides.title: The Big Race Day
slides.storyContext: Race day arrives. Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, averaging 5 m/s. Ravi takes 100 seconds (4 m/s). A cyclist passes them both, covering 600 meters in 60 seconds (10 m/s). Meera records all speeds and times.

example.problem: In the race: Amir (400 m, 80 s), Ravi (400 m, 100 s), Cyclist (600 m, 60 s). Find each one's speed. Who is fastest? If the cyclist had run 1 hour at that speed, how far would go?
example.solution: Amir: 5 m/s. Ravi: 4 m/s. Cyclist: 10 m/s. Cyclist is fastest. In 1 hour (3,600 s): 10 × 3,600 = 36,000 meters = 36 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each speed, compare, and use speed to predict distance over longer times.

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan the Training
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj asks Amir: 'If you improve to 6 m/s for the 400-meter race, what will your time be? And if I want you to run 1 kilometer at 5 m/s, how many seconds will that take?'

example.problem: At 6 m/s for 400 m, find time. At 5 m/s for 1 km (1,000 m), find time.
example.solution: Time for 400 m at 6 m/s: 400 ÷ 6 ≈ 66.7 seconds. Time for 1,000 m at 5 m/s: 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 seconds = 3 minutes 20 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use Time = Distance ÷ Speed to find how long a run takes.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: After the race, Amir sits with Coach Raj. 'I never knew math was the key to running fast,' Amir says. Coach smiles: 'Everything has math in it — racing, cooking, building, traveling.'

points.text: Time conversions: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Distance units: 1 km = 1,000 m. Measure distance in meters and kilometers.
Speed = Distance ÷ Time. A runner's speed is how far they go per unit time.
Distance = Speed × Time. Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Use these formulas to solve problems.
Compare speeds by calculating each one and seeing which is larger.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed, distance, and time are connected. Know any two, and you can find the third.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Animal Jumps: Data, Graphs, and Measurement
hook: Meera studies how far different animals can jump and organizes the data into tables and graphs.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: curious scientist who loves animals and collecting data

characters.name: Grandfather
characters.role: patient elder with encyclopedic knowledge of village animals

slides.title: Animal Jumps
slides.storyContext: Meera watches rabbits, frogs, grasshoppers, and dogs jumping in the village courtyard. 'How far can each one jump?' she wonders. She decides to measure and collect data to find out.

slides.title: Collecting Measurements
slides.storyContext: Meera marks a starting line with chalk and measures how far each animal jumps using a meter stick. Amir writes down the numbers: Rabbit 1: 2 m, Rabbit 2: 1.8 m, Frog 1: 0.6 m, Frog 2: 0.7 m, Grasshopper 1: 0.5 m, Grasshopper 2: 0.4 m, Dog 1: 1.5 m, Dog 2: 1.2 m. 'Now we organize this data,' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect by measuring or observing. We organize data into tables to see patterns.

slides.title: Measuring in Meters and Centimeters
slides.storyContext: Meera's rabbit jumps 2 meters. Another jumps 1 meter 80 centimeters (1.8 m). Grandfather explains: '1 meter = 100 centimeters. So 1 meter 80 centimeters is 180 centimeters total, or 1.8 meters.'

points.label: Meter-Centimeter Conversion
points.text: 1 meter = 100 centimeters. To convert meters to centimeters, multiply by 100. To convert centimeters to meters, divide by 100.

example.problem: A frog jumps 65 centimeters. Express this in meters.
example.solution: 65 cm ÷ 100 = 0.65 meters (or 65 cm = 0 m 65 cm).

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 meter = 100 cm. 1.5 meters = 150 cm. 80 cm = 0.8 meters.

image.alt: Measuring in Meters and Centimeters — Animal Jumps

slides.title: Creating a Data Table
slides.storyContext: Meera organizes the jump data into a clear table: Animal type, Number of jumps recorded, Average jump distance. Rabbit: 2, 1.9 m. Frog: 2, 0.65 m. Grasshopper: 2, 0.45 m. Dog: 2, 1.35 m. 'Now we can see which animal jumps farthest!'

points.label: Organizing Data in Tables
points.text: A table lists data in rows and columns. Rows are categories (animal type). Columns are measurements (distance, frequency, etc.). This makes it easy to compare and analyze.

example.problem: Create a table for: Rabbit 2 m, 1.8 m; Frog 0.6 m, 0.7 m. Calculate averages.
example.solution: Rabbit average: (2 + 1.8) ÷ 2 = 1.9 m. Frog average: (0.6 + 0.7) ÷ 2 = 0.65 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: A table organizes data so you can see patterns. Rows and columns make data easy to read and compare.

slides.title: Calculating Averages (Mean)
slides.storyContext: Meera has three grasshopper jump measurements: 0.5 m, 0.4 m, and 0.6 m. 'What's the average jump?' Amir adds: 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.5 m. Then divides by 3: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 m average.

points.label: Calculating the Mean (Average)
points.text: Add all the values, then divide by how many values there are. Average = (sum of all values) ÷ (number of values).

example.problem: Dog jumps: 1.5 m, 1.2 m, 1.4 m. What is the average?

slides.inSimpleWords: Average = sum of all values ÷ number of values. It tells you the typical value in a set.

slides.title: Creating a Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar graph on graph paper. The x-axis lists animals (Rabbit, Frog, Grasshopper, Dog). The y-axis shows distance in meters (0 to 2 m). She draws bars for each animal's average jump. The rabbit bar is tallest, the grasshopper bar shortest.

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: A bar graph uses rectangular bars to show data. The height of each bar represents a value. Bar graphs make it easy to compare values at a glance.

example.problem: Draw a bar graph for: Rabbit 1.9 m, Frog 0.65 m, Grasshopper 0.45 m, Dog 1.35 m.
example.solution: Create axes. X-axis: animal names. Y-axis: distance (0-2 m). Draw bars: Rabbit tallest, then Dog, then Frog, then Grasshopper.

slides.inSimpleWords: In a bar graph, taller bars mean bigger values. You can compare all values at once by looking at bar heights.

slides.title: Reading and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Looking at the bar graph, Meera asks: 'Which animal jumps the farthest? How much farther does a rabbit jump than a frog?' Amir reads: 'Rabbit jumps 1.9 m, frog jumps 0.65 m. Difference: 1.9 - 0.65 = 1.25 m.'

points.label: Analyzing Graphs
points.text: Read the axes carefully. Compare bar heights. Calculate differences and ratios if needed. Look for trends (is data increasing, decreasing, or stable?).

example.problem: From the bar graph: How much farther does a dog jump than a grasshopper?
example.solution: Dog: 1.35 m. Grasshopper: 0.45 m. Difference: 1.35 - 0.45 = 0.9 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read a graph by looking at the axes and comparing bar heights. You can calculate differences between values.

slides.title: The Complete Study
slides.storyContext: Meera writes a report: 'I measured jump distances for 4 animals. Rabbits jump the farthest (average 1.9 m), followed by dogs (1.35 m), frogs (0.65 m), and grasshoppers (0.45 m). I organized the data in a table and created a bar graph to show the comparison.'

example.problem: Create a full report: table, average calculations, and graph interpretation.
example.solution:
Table:
Animal | Jump 1 | Jump 2 | Average
Rabbit | 2.0 | 1.8 | 1.9
Frog | 0.6 | 0.7 | 0.65
Grasshopper | 0.5 | 0.4 | 0.45
Dog | 1.5 | 1.2 | 1.35

Interpretation: Rabbit jumps farthest; grasshopper jumps shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complete data analysis includes measurements, a table, averages, a graph, and conclusions.

slides.title: Your Turn: Analyze More Animals
slides.storyContext: Grandfather asks Meera: 'If a cat jumps 1.1 m and 1.3 m, what's its average? Where does it fit in your graph? Which animals jump twice as far as a grasshopper?'

example.problem: Cat jumps: 1.1 m, 1.3 m. Find average. Is it more or less than a dog's average (1.35 m)? Which animal jumps about 2× a grasshopper's distance (0.45 m)?
example.solution: Cat average: (1.1 + 1.3) ÷ 2 = 1.2 m. Less than dog's 1.35 m. 2 × grasshopper: 2 × 0.45 = 0.9 m ≈ dog's distance (1.35 m is close, but not exactly 2×; frog at 0.65 m is not 2×; rabbit at 1.9 m is 4.2×).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use averages and graphs to compare new data with existing data. Look for patterns and multiples.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Meera displays her poster with the data, graph, and conclusions at the village school fair. Grandfather smiles: 'You've learned to collect data, organize it, and tell a story with numbers and graphs.'

points.text: Measurement: use meters and centimeters; 1 m = 100 cm.
Data tables organize information in rows and columns for easy comparison.
Average (mean) = sum of values ÷ number of values. It represents a typical value.
Bar graphs use bar height to show values visually. Easy to compare at a glance.
Read graphs by checking axes, comparing heights, and calculating differences.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data, tables, and graphs help us understand the world. Measurements, organization, and analysis tell stories.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj and Priya's Village Map Adventure
hook: Help Raj and Priya find their way around the village using maps and directions.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Raj's clever cousin with a compass

slides.title: Maps and Locations
slides.storyContext: Raj and Priya arrive at their grandmother's village for summer holidays. Dadi pulls out an old hand-drawn map of the village and asks them to help find the local temple for evening prayers.
slides.inSimpleWords: A map is a picture that shows where things are in a place.

image.alt: Maps and Locations — Maps and Locations

slides.title: The Mystery of Dadi's Map
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows them her hand-drawn village map with the school, temple, marketplace, well, and her house marked. Raj gets excited: 'But Dadi, how do we know which way is north?' Priya pulls out a small compass from her pocket. Together, they realize the map has a compass rose drawn in the corner showing North, South, East, and West.
slides.inSimpleWords: Maps use directions like North, South, East, and West to show us how to get places.

image.alt: The Mystery of Dadi's Map — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Directions: The Four Cardinal Points
slides.storyContext: Standing in the middle of the village square, Dadi points: 'North is where the mountains are, South toward the river, East toward the sunrise, West toward the sunset.' Raj repeats the directions: North-East-South-West, and Priya adds, 'And we can remember it as NEWS!'

points.label: Cardinal Directions
points.text: North (N) = up, South (S) = down, East (E) = right (sunrise), West (W) = left (sunset)

points.label: Compass Rose
points.text: A symbol on the map showing these four directions

points.label: Finding your way
points.text: Always look for the compass rose to know which way to go

example.problem: If you are at Dadi's house facing the temple which is to the North, where would you turn to face the marketplace which is to the East?
example.solution: You would turn 90° to your right (clockwise) to face East.

slides.inSimpleWords: Directions help us know which way to go: North is up, South is down, East is right, West is left.

image.alt: Directions: The Four Cardinal Points — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Grid Lines: Making a Square Map
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a grid on Dadi's map using a ruler. 'Now we can find any place using rows and columns, like a checkerboard!' Each square in the grid is labeled. Dadi's house is in the square at Column B, Row 2. Raj picks a red crayon and marks it.

points.label: Grid
points.text: A pattern of lines that form squares on a map

points.label: Rows
points.text: Horizontal lines numbered from bottom (1) to top (for vertical position)

points.label: Columns
points.text: Vertical lines labeled A, B, C, D... from left to right (for horizontal position)

points.label: Grid Reference
points.text: Combining column letter and row number tells you exactly where something is

example.problem: The well is at column D, row 3. The school is at column B, row 4. Describe their positions on the grid.
example.solution: Well is in column D (4th column from left), row 3 (3rd row from bottom). School is in column B (2nd column from left), row 4 (4th row from bottom).

slides.inSimpleWords: A grid is like a checkerboard on the map. We use letters for columns and numbers for rows to pinpoint any location.

image.alt: Grid Lines: Making a Square Map — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Scale: Measuring Real Distances
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'Dadi, if the temple is just 1 cm away on your map, how far is it to really walk there?' Dadi smiles and points to the corner of her map: 'See this line marked 1 cm = 100 meters? That's the scale. So 1 cm on my map is 100 meters in real life.'

points.label: Map Scale
points.text: A ratio showing how map distance relates to real-world distance

points.label: Example scales
points.text: 1 cm = 100 m (small village), 1 cm = 1 km (larger area), 1 inch = 1 mile (very large areas)

points.label: Using scale
points.text: Measure the distance on the map, then multiply by the scale to find the real distance

example.problem: On Dadi's map, the distance from school to the marketplace is 3 cm. If the scale is 1 cm = 100 m, how far is it really?
example.solution: 3 cm × 100 m per cm = 300 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scale tells us how big real things actually are compared to the map. A small line on the map might mean a long walk in real life.

slides.title: Symbols on Maps: A Secret Code
slides.storyContext: Priya flips to the back of Dadi's map and finds a legend: a small temple symbol ⛩️, a school symbol 🏫, a house symbol 🏠, and a tree symbol 🌳. 'Dadi, this is like a secret code! Each symbol means something different,' she exclaims. Dadi nods: 'Yes, without the legend, we wouldn't know what we're looking at.'

points.label: Map Legend
points.text: A key that explains what each symbol or color on the map means

points.label: Common symbols
points.text: Houses (small squares), schools (flag), temples (spire), trees (green dots), rivers (blue wavy lines)

points.label: Why symbols?
points.text: Drawing real pictures would make the map too crowded; symbols are simple and clear

example.problem: On a map legend, you see: ⛩️ = temple, 🏥 = health center, 💧 = well. If there are 3 wells marked on the map, how many sources of water does the village have?
example.solution: At least 3, though there may be more wells not marked on the map.

slides.inSimpleWords: Map symbols are like a picture code. A legend tells you what each symbol means.

slides.title: Different Types of Maps
slides.storyContext: At Dadi's house, Raj finds three different maps in a drawer: a hand-drawn village map (physical features like rivers and trees), a road map with marked routes, and a thematic map showing where crops grow. 'Which one is best?' he asks. Priya says, 'They show different things! We choose based on what we need to find.'

points.label: Physical Maps
points.text: Show natural features: rivers, mountains, forests, valleys

points.label: Political Maps
points.text: Show borders, states, cities, countries

points.label: Road/Street Maps
points.text: Show streets, highways, landmarks for navigation

points.label: Thematic Maps
points.text: Show specific information like weather, population, or crop distribution

slides.inSimpleWords: Different maps show different information. Pick the right map for what you want to find out.

slides.title: Reading Dadi's Village Map: A Full Task
slides.storyContext: Now Raj and Priya are ready for the real challenge. Dadi hands them the village map and asks them to plan a route from her house to the marketplace, passing by the school. They use the grid references, cardinal directions, and the scale to plan their walk.

example.problem: Using the village map (scale: 1 cm = 100 m, grid shown), Dadi's house is at B2, the school is at C3, and the marketplace is at D2. Plan a route and calculate the total walking distance. Which direction from school leads to the marketplace?
example.solution: Route: Start at B2 (Dadi's house) → go East and North to C3 (school) → then go East and South to D2 (marketplace). Direction from school to market: East and South (Southeast). Distance: approximately 2.5 cm on map = 250 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading a map means using the grid, directions, and scale together to find places and measure distances.

slides.title: Can You Find the Hidden Well?
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives Raj and Priya a challenge before dinner: 'There's a well hidden on the eastern edge of the village. It's 2 cm from the marketplace according to the scale. Can you find it on the map?' Raj and Priya work together, measuring, looking at the scale, and checking the compass rose.

example.problem: Starting from the marketplace at D2, go 2 cm due East (right) on a map with scale 1 cm = 100 m. What is the real distance, and approximately at which grid position should the well be?
example.solution: Real distance: 2 cm × 100 m/cm = 200 meters. The well would be approximately at E2 on the grid (one column to the right, same row).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using a map, you can find hidden places by following directions and using the scale.

slides.title: What We Learned Today
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Raj and Priya sit with Dadi, proudly holding the map. 'We found everything we needed,' says Priya. Dadi smiles: 'You learned to read a map like true explorers.'

points.label: Directions
points.text: North, South, East, West (NEWS) help us know which way to go

points.label: Grid
points.text: Columns (letters) and rows (numbers) pinpoint exact locations

points.label: Scale
points.text: Tells us how map distance relates to real distance

points.label: Symbols & Legend
points.text: A key code that explains what each symbol means

points.label: Map Types
points.text: Different maps show different information; choose the right one for your need

slides.inSimpleWords: Maps are tools that help us find our way. With directions, a grid, scale, and symbols, we can navigate anywhere.
